newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Sharif confident of victory in Pakistan elections.
newsitem.headline: Sharif confident of victory in Pakistan elections.

text.p: Nawaz Sharif, tipped to become Pakistan's next prime minister, said before casting his vote on Monday that he would seek to cooperate with his main rival Benazir Bhutto, rather than putting her on trial.
"We are not going to indulge in any politics of revenge. No politics of confrontation," he told Reuters at his home in the industrial city of Lahore, provincial capital of Punjab.

"It will be clean, good politics and we'll try to seek her cooperation to take the country forward because it is essential now we are preparing to enter the 21st century and we want to enter it with dignity and honour.
"Therefore, I think the opposition and the government must have some rapport, some working relationship. So, what she did to us, we will not do to her," he said.
Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML) party accused Bhutto's government of victimisation during its three years in power.

President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto on November 5 for alleged corruption, installing a caretaker government which is widely reported to have prepared, but not filed, corruption charges against her and her jailed husband, Asif Ali Zardari.
Sharif, whose last government was dismissed by a former president on similar charges in 1993, said he would strengthen a commission set up by the caretaker government to fight graft.
"We'll we see that the commission is free of any government influences," he declared.
Sharif rejected the view that Pakistanis were fed up with politicians in general, blaming Bhutto for public discontent.
"The politicians have not made any mess. If anyone has made a mess, it is Benazir Bhutto in the past three years," he said.
"She brought a bad name to politics. She brought a bad name to politicians. And she also brought a bad name to parliament."
Sharif, an industrialist perceived as pro-business, said Pakistan's image could change "overnight" given good governance.
He said he was confident of winning a comfortable majority in the 217-seat National Assembly (lower house) and forming a stable government.
"The country needs a strong and stable government and the problems that we have on our hands, I think only a strong and stable government can solve," he said.
Sharif, who later drove to vote at a polling station in a muddy lane in Lahore's old city, said he did not share widespread expectations of a low turn-out by apathetic voters.
"You'll see the result today. And today is the day of real accountability," he told reporters crushed around him.
Sharif said he looked forward to a cooperative relationship with Leghari, a former Bhutto loyalist.

"I think the confrontation between the prime minister and the president must end now," he said. "We've had enough of confrontation between these two. The president and the prime minister must learn to work together."
But he denied media reports and accusations by political foes that he has already reached an understanding with Leghari.
"Why should I make a deal? If I were to make any deal, I'd make it with the people of Pakistan," he said.
